name: Nasal irrigation

card.summary: Saline rinsing of the nose, used for congestion and sinus symptoms; looksmaxxing interest centres on clearing congestion, with no studies of its effect on nose appearance.
card.aka: Neti pot, nasal lavage, sinus rinse, jala neti
card.note: Guidance stresses sterile, distilled or previously boiled water; contaminated water has been linked to rare serious infections.

quick.overview:
Nasal irrigation flushes the nasal passages with salt water using a neti pot, squeeze bottle or similar device. It is an established practice with roots in Ayurvedic tradition and is recommended in some guidelines as an adjunct for sinus and allergy symptoms.

It is listed here because people interested in nasal appearance and breathing discuss it for clearing congestion. No published study examines whether irrigation changes how the nose looks.
quick.mechanism: A saline solution is passed through one nostril and out the other, which moistens the mucosa and flushes mucus, allergens and debris. Studies have examined how well different devices distribute fluid within the sinuses.
quick.risks: Reviews describe irritation, stinging and nosebleeds as the usual side effects. Rare fatal infections, including amoeba infections, have followed use of untreated tap water, and health agencies advise sterile, distilled or boiled and cooled water and cleaning of devices.

lead: Nasal irrigation, also called nasal lavage or neti pot use, is a hygiene and medical practice that rinses the nasal cavity with a saline solution to remove mucus and debris [1][2]. It originated in Ayurvedic practice in India, where jala neti is traditionally part of daily personal hygiene [1][2].

Medical evidence is strongest for symptom relief. A 2015 guideline cited by Wikipedia supports irrigation for symptoms of acute sinusitis, a 2016 Cochrane review is reported to find weak evidence for chronic sinusitis, and a 2012 meta-analysis suggests temporary relief in allergic rhinitis [1]. Grokipedia describes guidelines and systematic reviews as supportive for chronic rhinosinusitis and allergic rhinitis [2].

The wiki includes the entry because clearing a blocked nose is discussed in communities concerned with nasal breathing and appearance. No study cited here tests irrigation as an appearance intervention.
infobox: Neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe, powered irrigator [1]
Use sterile, distilled or boiled and cooled water [1]

paras: Common devices are neti pots, squeeze bottles, bulb syringes (often for children) and electric irrigators. Saline is poured or pumped through one nostril and drains from the other [1]. Isotonic (0.9 percent) or hypertonic saline is used, and high-volume, low-pressure delivery is described as typical [2].

Laboratory studies compared how neti pots, squeeze bottles and pressurised sprays distribute solution in cadaver sinuses after endoscopic sinus surgery [3]. Computational and 3D-printed model studies simulate how irrigation fluid fills and coats the nasal airway [4][5][6].

Wikipedia reports that irrigation is generally well tolerated, with possible irritation, nosebleeds, headache and post-rinse drainage [1]. The main concern is infection from non-sterile water or unwashed devices. Fatal cases of amoebic infection linked to tap-water neti pot use were reported in 2011 and 2013, and a 2018 case involved Balamuthia infection after tap water filtered through a household purifier [1]. A case report describes pneumococcal meningitis associated with over-the-counter sinus irrigation [7].

The US CDC guidance as summarised by Wikipedia advises water that is boiled for one minute and cooled, filtered to a stated standard, or labelled distilled or sterile [1]. Grokipedia lists the same measures and advises cleaning devices after each use [2]. Research has also examined how much irrigation fluid remains in the nose and how medicines added to irrigation are absorbed [8].

Evidence summarised in encyclopedic sources relates to sinus and allergy symptoms, including a 2015 guideline, a 2016 Cochrane review and a 2012 meta-analysis [1], and a review covers irrigation after endoscopic sinus surgery [9]. Cadaver, computational and 3D-printed model studies address fluid distribution rather than patient outcomes [3][4][5][6]. No studies found on nasal irrigation as a way of changing the visible appearance of the nose.

Nasal irrigation sits in the sleep and breathing category of this wiki because congestion is discussed as something that can swell or distort the look of the nose and affect breathing. The discussion is not documented in the sources cited here, and no published research links irrigation to a change in nasal appearance.
